It really impacts my daily interactions because I worry it makes me look impatient or like I'm not truly listening.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your symptoms of restlessness, impulsivity, and difficulty waiting for your turn have impacted your daily life and relationships, and have you noticed any significant differences in how these symptoms affect you in different settings or situations?\n\nPatient: In my past startup roles, my high energy and multitasking were tolerated, but in my current senior role, these issues have led to negative performance reviews and being passed over for key projects. This is actually the first time I've ever sought out any kind of psychiatric evaluation or mental health treatment.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned that these symptoms have been present since childhood, but can you tell me if there was ever a period in your life where your symptoms significantly improved or decreased, even if temporarily?\n\nPatient: I don't think there was ever a time they truly went away or improved. However, they were definitely less of a problem and easier to manage when I was working in fast-paced startup environments doing hands-on coding.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that your symptoms have been present since childhood, but can you clarify if you've experienced any periods of significant improvement or worsening of these symptoms during adolescence or early adulthood, before your current senior role?\n\nPatient: I don't recall any specific periods of significant improvement or worsening during my adolescence or early adulthood. I think I mostly just got by because my environments, like school and my earlier startup jobs, naturally allowed me to stay active and multitask.\n\nDoctor: Can you compare the severity of your symptoms, such as restlessness and impulsivity, in childhood versus adulthood, and how have they impacted your functioning in different life settings?\n\nPatient: In childhood, the symptoms were highly visible, with teachers constantly complaining that I couldn't stay in my seat, walked around, and blurted out answers. Now, leaving my seat in long meetings and interrupting in one-on-ones has seriously impacted my professional functioning, leading to negative performance reviews and missed career opportunities.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe any instances where you engaged in physical activities that could be considered excessive or inappropriate for the setting, such as running or climbing in inappropriate situations?\n\nPatient: I don't literally run or climb on things anymore as an adult, but I experience the adult equivalent, which is an intense, pent-up physical restlessness. Even waiting in line at a coffee shop makes me really impatient and constantly shift around.\n\nDoctor: Do you also find it difficult to focus on tasks or activities, such as reading a book or following a conversation, and do you often find yourself easily distracted?\n\nPatient: Yes, definitely. On longer Zoom calls, my mind often drifts off to other projects or dinner plans within ten minutes, and I'll suddenly realize I've missed a big chunk of the conversation. I also get easily sidetracked; if I'm working on a multi-step task, a new email can completely derail me and I'll forget to finish the last steps.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever acted on impulses, such as blurting out answers or interrupting others, without fully thinking them through, and if so, how often does this happen?\n\nPatient: Yes, this happens a lot, especially in one-on-one meetings with my engineers. My brain races ahead, and I constantly find myself jumping in with solutions or finishing their sentences before they can even finish explaining the problem. I just get this really strong urge to say it right away.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about how often you experience feelings of impulsivity, such as interrupting others or blurting out answers, compared to the restlessness and need to move around that you've described?\n\nPatient: Both happen very frequently, but they show up in different situations. The impulsivity of blurting out answers or finishing sentences happens constantly during one-on-one discussions when my brain is racing ahead. In contrast, the physical restlessness and urge to fidget or get up is a constant struggle whenever I am forced to sit still for more than 15 to 30 minutes, especially in those longer, structured meetings.\n\nDoctor: Do you find that your impulsivity, such as interrupting others, tends to occur more frequently in situations where you're also feeling restless and need to move around, or are these two symptoms relatively separate for you?\n\nPatient: I haven't really thought about whether the two are directly connected, since they seem to show up in different moments. The interrupting usually happens during fast-paced, one-on-one discussions when my brain is racing ahead, whereas the restlessness and urge to move tend to build up during those long, passive meetings where I just have to sit still.\n\nDoctor: Do you often have difficulty waiting for your turn or doing things in sequence, such as waiting in line or taking turns in a conversation, and if so, how does this impact your daily life?\n\nPatient: Yes, I struggle a lot with waiting my turn; standing in lines makes me incredibly impatient, so I'm constantly shifting around and checking my phone. In conversations, especially one-on-ones, I frequently jump in with solutions or finish my engineers' sentences because my mind races ahead and I feel an urgent need to speak. It really impacts my daily interactions because I worry it makes me look impatient or like I'm not truly listening.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your symptoms of restlessness, impulsivity, and difficulty waiting for your turn have impacted your daily life and relationships, and have you noticed any significant differences in how these symptoms affect you in different settings or situations?\n\nPatient: In my past startup roles, my high energy and multitasking were tolerated, but in my current senior role, these issues have led to negative performance reviews and being passed over for key projects. Professionally, interrupting my engineers in one-on-ones strains those relationships, while personally, the extreme jitteriness during my kids' school assemblies or waiting in lines makes it hard to just relax. It is definitely much harder to manage now in these highly structured environments compared to when I was just doing hands-on coding.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me at what age you first started noticing these symptoms of restlessness, impulsivity, and difficulty waiting for your turn, and have they been present consistently throughout your life?\n\nPatient: Yes, they have actually been present since I was a child. Back in elementary school, teachers were always telling my parents that I couldn't stay in my seat, blurted out answers, and constantly walked around the classroom when I was supposed to be working quietly. It's definitely been a consistent, lifelong pattern for me.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been diagnosed with or treated for any other conditions, such as mood disorders, anxiety disorders, or learning disorders, that could be contributing to your symptoms of inattention and impulsivity?\n\nPatient: No, I have never been diagnosed with or treated for any other conditions like anxiety, mood disorders, or learning disabilities. This is actually the first time I've ever sought out any kind of psychiatric evaluation or mental health treatment.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned that these symptoms have been present since childhood, but can you tell me if there was ever a period in your life where your symptoms significantly improved or decreased, even if temporarily?\n\nPatient: I don't think there was ever a time they truly went away or improved. However, they were definitely less of a problem and easier to manage when I was working in fast-paced startup environments doing hands-on coding.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that your symptoms have been present since childhood, but can you clarify if you've experienced any periods of significant improvement or worsening of these symptoms during adolescence or early adulthood, before your current senior role?\n\nPatient: I don't recall any specific periods of significant improvement or worsening during my adolescence or early adulthood. I think I mostly just got by because my environments, like school and my earlier startup jobs, naturally allowed me to stay active and multitask.\n\nDoctor: Can you compare the severity of your symptoms, such as restlessness and impulsivity, in childhood versus adulthood, and how have they impacted your functioning in different life settings?\n\nPatient: In childhood, the symptoms were highly visible, with teachers constantly complaining that I couldn't stay in my seat, walked around, and blurted out answers. As an adult, I coped well for years in fast-paced coding roles, but since my promotion two years ago, the restlessness and impulsivity have resurfaced as major issues. Now, leaving my seat in long meetings and interrupting in one-on-ones has seriously impacted my professional functioning, leading to negative performance reviews and missed career opportunities.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe any instances where you engaged in physical activities that could be considered excessive or inappropriate for the setting, such as running or climbing in inappropriate situations?\n\nPatient: I don't literally run or climb on things anymore as an adult, but I experience the adult equivalent, which is an intense, pent-up physical restlessness. During long meetings or my kids' school assemblies, I get this jittery feeling like I'm going to crawl out of my skin, forcing me to constantly get up, stretch, or pace around.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your symptoms have impacted your social relationships, such as friendships and romantic relationships, and have you noticed any differences in how your symptoms affect these relationships compared to your professional relationships?\n\nPatient: Honestly, I haven't really noticed a major impact on my personal friendships or romantic relationships. My friends and family are quite used to my high energy, so the difficulties I've been experiencing are almost entirely focused on my professional life and work environment.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your difficulties with restlessness and impulsivity are more prominent than your difficulties with inattention and disorganization, or are they equally problematic for you?\n\nPatient: The restlessness and impulsivity—specifically my constant urge to leave my seat during meetings and my habit of jumping in with answers—are definitely much more prominent and cause the most disruption at work. While I do also struggle with my attention drifting and organizing my weekly tasks, those issues feel secondary to the physical need to move.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate the proportion of your daily life where you feel your restlessness and impulsivity symptoms are under control versus when they are problematic, and how does this impact your overall functioning?\n\nPatient: When I am doing hands-on coding, I feel completely in control, but since transitioning to my senior role two years ago, a large portion of my day is filled with long meetings where my restlessness is highly problematic. This has really impacted my functioning at work, leading to performance reviews noting that I seem distracted and disengaged. I've even been passed over for leading high-visibility projects because of how I come across in those sessions.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your symptoms of restlessness and impulsivity have caused more significant problems in your life compared to symptoms of inattention, or are they equally troublesome for you?\n\nPatient: The restlessness and impulsivity are definitely more troublesome because they are highly visible and have directly harmed my professional reputation, leading to me being passed over for leadership roles when I leave my seat or blurt out answers. In contrast, my inattention symptoms, like drifting off during Zoom calls, are frustrating but feel much more internal and are easier to hide from my colleagues.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify whether your symptoms of restlessness and impulsivity have caused significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning, and if so, to what extent?\n\nPatient: Yes, they have caused significant occupational impairment over the last two years. My performance reviews have started to note that I seem distracted and not fully present in meetings because of my restlessness. I've even been passed over to lead high-visibility projects because my managers worry about how I come across during long planning sessions.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your restlessness and impulsivity symptoms would be considered mild, moderate, or severe in terms of how much they interfere with your daily life and work, and can you give me some specific examples to support your answer?"
  }

Professionally, interrupting my engineers in one-on-ones strains those relationships, while personally, the extreme jitteriness during my kids' school assemblies or waiting in lines makes it hard to just relax. It is definitely much harder to manage now in these highly structured environments compared to when I was just doing hands-on coding.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me at what age you first started noticing these symptoms of restlessness, impulsivity, and difficulty waiting for your turn, and have they been present consistently throughout your life?\n\nPatient: Yes, they have actually been present since I was a child. Back in elementary school, teachers were always telling my parents that I couldn't stay in my seat, blurted out answers, and constantly walked around the classroom when I was supposed to be working quietly. It's definitely been a consistent, lifelong pattern for me.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been diagnosed with or treated for any other conditions, such as mood disorders, anxiety disorders, or learning disorders, that could be contributing to your symptoms of inattention and impulsivity?\n\nPatient: No, I have never been diagnosed with or treated for any other conditions like anxiety, mood disorders, or learning disabilities. This is actually the first time I've ever sought out any kind of psychiatric evaluation or mental health treatment.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned that these symptoms have been present since childhood, but can you tell me if there was ever a period in your life where your symptoms significantly improved or decreased, even if temporarily?\n\nPatient: I don't think there was ever a time they truly went away or improved. However, they were definitely less of a problem and easier to manage when I was working in fast-paced startup environments doing hands-on coding.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that your symptoms have been present since childhood, but can you clarify if you've experienced any periods of significant improvement or worsening of these symptoms during adolescence or early adulthood, before your current senior role?\n\nPatient: I don't recall any specific periods of significant improvement or worsening during my adolescence or early adulthood. I think I mostly just got by because my environments, like school and my earlier startup jobs, naturally allowed me to stay active and multitask.\n\nDoctor: Can you compare the severity of your symptoms, such as restlessness and impulsivity, in childhood versus adulthood, and how have they impacted your functioning in different life settings?\n\nPatient: In childhood, the symptoms were highly visible, with teachers constantly complaining that I couldn't stay in my seat, walked around, and blurted out answers. As an adult, I coped well for years in fast-paced coding roles, but since my promotion two years ago, the restlessness and impulsivity have resurfaced as major issues. Now, leaving my seat in long meetings and interrupting in one-on-ones has seriously impacted my professional functioning, leading to negative performance reviews and missed career opportunities.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe any instances where you engaged in physical activities that could be considered excessive or inappropriate for the setting, such as running or climbing in inappropriate situations?\n\nPatient: I don't literally run or climb on things anymore as an adult, but I experience the adult equivalent, which is an intense, pent-up physical restlessness. During long meetings or my kids' school assemblies, I get this jittery feeling like I'm going to crawl out of my skin, forcing me to constantly get up, stretch, or pace around.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your symptoms have impacted your social relationships, such as friendships and romantic relationships, and have you noticed any differences in how your symptoms affect these relationships compared to your professional relationships?\n\nPatient: Honestly, I haven't really noticed a major impact on my personal friendships or romantic relationships. My friends and family are quite used to my high energy, so the difficulties I've been experiencing are almost entirely focused on my professional life and work environment.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your difficulties with restlessness and impulsivity are more prominent than your difficulties with inattention and disorganization, or are they equally problematic for you?\n\nPatient: The restlessness and impulsivity—specifically my constant urge to leave my seat during meetings and my habit of jumping in with answers—are definitely much more prominent and cause the most disruption at work. While I do also struggle with my attention drifting and organizing my weekly tasks, those issues feel secondary to the physical need to move.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate the proportion of your daily life where you feel your restlessness and impulsivity symptoms are under control versus when they are problematic, and how does this impact your overall functioning?\n\nPatient: When I am doing hands-on coding, I feel completely in control, but since transitioning to my senior role two years ago, a large portion of my day is filled with long meetings where my restlessness is highly problematic. This has really impacted my functioning at work, leading to performance reviews noting that I seem distracted and disengaged. I've even been passed over for leading high-visibility projects because of how I come across in those sessions.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your symptoms of restlessness and impulsivity have caused more significant problems in your life compared to symptoms of inattention, or are they equally troublesome for you?\n\nPatient: The restlessness and impulsivity are definitely more troublesome because they are highly visible and have directly harmed my professional reputation, leading to me being passed over for leadership roles when I leave my seat or blurt out answers. In contrast, my inattention symptoms, like drifting off during Zoom calls, are frustrating but feel much more internal and are easier to hide from my colleagues.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify whether your symptoms of restlessness and impulsivity have caused significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning, and if so, to what extent?\n\nPatient: Yes, they have caused significant occupational impairment over the last two years. My performance reviews have started to note that I seem distracted and not fully present in meetings because of my restlessness. I've even been passed over to lead high-visibility projects because my managers worry about how I come across during long planning sessions.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your restlessness and impulsivity symptoms would be considered mild, moderate, or severe in terms of how much they interfere with your daily life and work, and can you give me some specific examples to support your answer?\n\nPatient: I would consider my symptoms to be mild overall, but they have recently caused noticeable setbacks at work. Specifically, my performance reviews have noted that I seem distracted or not fully present in meetings, and I've been passed over for leading high-visibility projects because my managers worry about my presence during long planning sessions.\n\nDoctor: Can you elaborate on what you mean by considering your symptoms 'mild overall' despite acknowledging they have caused significant occupational impairment and impacted your professional reputation?\n\nPatient: I consider them mild because I am still highly capable and very successful at my core technical work, like hands-on coding. They only feel significant now because my new senior role demands long, structured meetings and leadership presence, which clash with these lifelong traits and have caused these recent setbacks.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if there are any specific situations or environments where your symptoms of restlessness and impulsivity are less problematic, and if so, what factors in those situations help mitigate their impact?"

It’s started to impact how my colleagues and managers perceive me in my new senior role, so I wanted to get some professional advice on how to handle it.\n\nDoctor: Do you experience these feelings of restlessness and need to move around in other situations as well, such as when you're at home or in more relaxed settings?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely. If I have to sit still for more than half an hour, like at my kids' school assemblies, I get this pent-up, jittery feeling like I'm going to crawl out of my skin. Even waiting in line at a coffee shop makes me really impatient and constantly shift around.\n\nDoctor: Do you also find it difficult to focus on tasks or activities, such as reading a book or following a conversation, and do you often find yourself easily distracted?\n\nPatient: Yes, definitely. On longer Zoom calls, my mind often drifts off to other projects or dinner plans within ten minutes, and I'll suddenly realize I've missed a big chunk of the conversation. I also get easily sidetracked; if I'm working on a multi-step task, a new email can completely derail me and I'll forget to finish the last steps.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever acted on impulses, such as blurting out answers or interrupting others, without fully thinking them through, and if so, how often does this happen?\n\nPatient: Yes, this happens a lot, especially in one-on-one meetings with my engineers. My brain races ahead, and I constantly find myself jumping in with solutions or finishing their sentences before they can even finish explaining the problem. I just get this really strong urge to say it right away.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about how often you experience feelings of impulsivity, such as interrupting others or blurting out answers, compared to the restlessness and need to move around that you've described?\n\nPatient: Both happen very frequently, but they show up in different situations. The impulsivity of blurting out answers or finishing sentences happens constantly during one-on-one discussions when my brain is racing ahead. In contrast, the physical restlessness and urge to fidget or get up is a constant struggle whenever I am forced to sit still for more than 15 to 30 minutes, especially in those longer, structured meetings.\n\nDoctor: Do you find that your impulsivity, such as interrupting others, tends to occur more frequently in situations where you're also feeling restless and need to move around, or are these two symptoms relatively separate for you?\n\nPatient: I haven't really thought about whether the two are directly connected, since they seem to show up in different moments. The interrupting usually happens during fast-paced, one-on-one discussions when my brain is racing ahead, whereas the restlessness and urge to move tend to build up during those long, passive meetings where I just have to sit still.\n\nDoctor: Do you often have difficulty waiting for your turn or doing things in sequence, such as waiting in line or taking turns in a conversation, and if so, how does this impact your daily life?\n\nPatient: Yes, I struggle a lot with waiting my turn; standing in lines makes me incredibly impatient, so I'm constantly shifting around and checking my phone. In conversations, especially one-on-ones, I frequently jump in with solutions or finish my engineers' sentences because my mind races ahead and I feel an urgent need to speak. It really impacts my daily interactions because I worry it makes me look impatient or like I'm not truly listening.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your symptoms of restlessness, impulsivity, and difficulty waiting for your turn have impacted your daily life and relationships, and have you noticed any significant differences in how these symptoms affect you in different settings or situations?\n\nPatient: In my past startup roles, my high energy and multitasking were tolerated, but in my current senior role, these issues have led to negative performance reviews and being passed over for key projects. Professionally, interrupting my engineers in one-on-ones strains those relationships, while personally, the extreme jitteriness during my kids' school assemblies or waiting in lines makes it hard to just relax. It is definitely much harder to manage now in these highly structured environments compared to when I was just doing hands-on coding.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me at what age you first started noticing these symptoms of restlessness, impulsivity, and difficulty waiting for your turn, and have they been present consistently throughout your life?\n\nPatient: Yes, they have actually been present since I was a child. Back in elementary school, teachers were always telling my parents that I couldn't stay in my seat, blurted out answers, and constantly walked around the classroom when I was supposed to be working quietly. It's definitely been a consistent, lifelong pattern for me.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been diagnosed with or treated for any other conditions, such as mood disorders, anxiety disorders, or learning disorders, that could be contributing to your symptoms of inattention and impulsivity?\n\nPatient: No, I have never been diagnosed with or treated for any other conditions like anxiety, mood disorders, or learning disabilities. This is actually the first time I've ever sought out any kind of psychiatric evaluation or mental health treatment.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned that these symptoms have been present since childhood, but can you tell me if there was ever a period in your life where your symptoms significantly improved or decreased, even if temporarily?\n\nPatient: I don't think there was ever a time they truly went away or improved. However, they were definitely less of a problem and easier to manage when I was working in fast-paced startup environments doing hands-on coding.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that your symptoms have been present since childhood, but can you clarify if you've experienced any periods of significant improvement or worsening of these symptoms during adolescence or early adulthood, before your current senior role?\n\nPatient: I don't recall any specific periods of significant improvement or worsening during my adolescence or early adulthood. I think I mostly just got by because my environments, like school and my earlier startup jobs, naturally allowed me to stay active and multitask.\n\nDoctor: Can you compare the severity of your symptoms, such as restlessness and impulsivity, in childhood versus adulthood, and how have they impacted your functioning in different life settings?\n\nPatient: In childhood, the symptoms were highly visible, with teachers constantly complaining that I couldn't stay in my seat, walked around, and blurted out answers. As an adult, I coped well for years in fast-paced coding roles, but since my promotion two years ago, the restlessness and impulsivity have resurfaced as major issues. Now, leaving my seat in long meetings and interrupting in one-on-ones has seriously impacted my professional functioning, leading to negative performance reviews and missed career opportunities.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe any instances where you engaged in physical activities that could be considered excessive or inappropriate for the setting, such as running or climbing in inappropriate situations?\n\nPatient: I don't literally run or climb on things anymore as an adult, but I experience the adult equivalent, which is an intense, pent-up physical restlessness. During long meetings or my kids' school assemblies, I get this jittery feeling like I'm going to crawl out of my skin, forcing me to constantly get up, stretch, or pace around.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your symptoms have impacted your social relationships, such as friendships and romantic relationships, and have you noticed any differences in how your symptoms affect these relationships compared to your professional relationships?\n\nPatient: Honestly, I haven't really noticed a major impact on my personal friendships or romantic relationships. My friends and family are quite used to my high energy, so the difficulties I've been experiencing are almost entirely focused on my professional life and work environment.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your difficulties with restlessness and impulsivity are more prominent than your difficulties with inattention and disorganization, or are they equally problematic for you?\n\nPatient: The restlessness and impulsivity—specifically my constant urge to leave my seat during meetings and my habit of jumping in with answers—are definitely much more prominent and cause the most disruption at work. While I do also struggle with my attention drifting and organizing my weekly tasks, those issues feel secondary to the physical need to move.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate the proportion of your daily life where you feel your restlessness and impulsivity symptoms are under control versus when they are problematic, and how does this impact your overall functioning?\n\nPatient: When I am doing hands-on coding, I feel completely in control, but since transitioning to my senior role two years ago, a large portion of my day is filled with long meetings where my restlessness is highly problematic. This has really impacted my functioning at work, leading to performance reviews noting that I seem distracted and disengaged. I've even been passed over for leading high-visibility projects because of how I come across in those sessions.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your symptoms of restlessness and impulsivity have caused more significant problems in your life compared to symptoms of inattention, or are they equally troublesome for you?\n\nPatient: The restlessness and impulsivity are definitely more troublesome because they are highly visible and have directly harmed my professional reputation, leading to me being passed over for leadership roles when I leave my seat or blurt out answers. In contrast, my inattention symptoms, like drifting off during Zoom calls, are frustrating but feel much more internal and are easier to hide from my colleagues.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify whether your symptoms of restlessness and impulsivity have caused significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning, and if so, to what extent?\n\nPatient: Yes, they have caused significant occupational impairment over the last two years. My performance reviews have started to note that I seem distracted and not fully present in meetings because of my restlessness. I've even been passed over to lead high-visibility projects because my managers worry about how I come across during long planning sessions.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your restlessness and impulsivity symptoms would be considered mild, moderate, or severe in terms of how much they interfere with your daily life and work, and can you give me some specific examples to support your answer?\n\nPatient: I would consider my symptoms to be mild overall, but they have recently caused noticeable setbacks at work. Specifically, my performance reviews have noted that I seem distracted or not fully present in meetings, and I've been passed over for leading high-visibility projects because my managers worry about my presence during long planning sessions.\n\nDoctor: Can you elaborate on what you mean by considering your symptoms 'mild overall' despite acknowledging they have caused significant occupational impairment and impacted your professional reputation?\n\nPatient: I consider them mild because I am still highly capable and very successful at my core technical work, like hands-on coding. They only feel significant now because my new senior role demands long, structured meetings and leadership presence, which clash with these lifelong traits and have caused these recent setbacks.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if there are any specific situations or environments where your symptoms of restlessness and impulsivity are less problematic, and if so, what factors in those situations help mitigate their impact?\n\nPatient: My symptoms were much less of a problem when I was doing hands-on software development, particularly in fast-paced startup environments. The coding and rapid problem-solving kept me highly engaged, and my tendencies to pace, move around, and multitask were tolerated and didn't interfere with my performance. It's only in these long, structured planning meetings in my new role that it has become a real issue.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about how often you experience feelings of physical restlessness versus impulsive behaviors, and are there any specific situations where one is more prominent than the other?\n\nPatient: My physical restlessness is most prominent when I am forced to sit still for long periods, like during all-hands meetings or school assemblies, where I get a pent-up, jittery feeling. In contrast, my impulsive behaviors show up more in interactive settings, like blurting out answers and finishing sentences during one-on-ones, or feeling highly impatient when waiting to speak in groups or standing in lines.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your impulsivity, such as blurting out answers, is more of a problem for you than your hyperactivity, or are they equally troublesome in your daily life and work?"

Even waiting in line at a coffee shop makes me really impatient and constantly shift around.\n\nDoctor: Do you also find it difficult to focus on tasks or activities, such as reading a book or following a conversation, and do you often find yourself easily distracted?\n\nPatient: Yes, definitely. On longer Zoom calls, my mind often drifts off to other projects or dinner plans within ten minutes, and I'll suddenly realize I've missed a big chunk of the conversation. I also get easily sidetracked; if I'm working on a multi-step task, a new email can completely derail me and I'll forget to finish the last steps.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever acted on impulses, such as blurting out answers or interrupting others, without fully thinking them through, and if so, how often does this happen?\n\nPatient: Yes, this happens a lot, especially in one-on-one meetings with my engineers. My brain races ahead, and I constantly find myself jumping in with solutions or finishing their sentences before they can even finish explaining the problem. I just get this really strong urge to say it right away.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about how often you experience feelings of impulsivity, such as interrupting others or blurting out answers, compared to the restlessness and need to move around that you've described?\n\nPatient: Both happen very frequently, but they show up in different situations. The impulsivity of blurting out answers or finishing sentences happens constantly during one-on-one discussions when my brain is racing ahead. In contrast, the physical restlessness and urge to fidget or get up is a constant struggle whenever I am forced to sit still for more than 15 to 30 minutes, especially in those longer, structured meetings.\n\nDoctor: Do you find that your impulsivity, such as interrupting others, tends to occur more frequently in situations where you're also feeling restless and need to move around, or are these two symptoms relatively separate for you?\n\nPatient: I haven't really thought about whether the two are directly connected, since they seem to show up in different moments. The interrupting usually happens during fast-paced, one-on-one discussions when my brain is racing ahead, whereas the restlessness and urge to move tend to build up during those long, passive meetings where I just have to sit still.\n\nDoctor: Do you often have difficulty waiting for your turn or doing things in sequence, such as waiting in line or taking turns in a conversation, and if so, how does this impact your daily life?\n\nPatient: Yes, I struggle a lot with waiting my turn; standing in lines makes me incredibly impatient, so I'm constantly shifting around and checking my phone. In conversations, especially one-on-ones, I frequently jump in with solutions or finish my engineers' sentences because my mind races ahead and I feel an urgent need to speak. It really impacts my daily interactions because I worry it makes me look impatient or like I'm not truly listening.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your symptoms of restlessness, impulsivity, and difficulty waiting for your turn have impacted your daily life and relationships, and have you noticed any significant differences in how these symptoms affect you in different settings or situations?\n\nPatient: In my past startup roles, my high energy and multitasking were tolerated, but in my current senior role, these issues have led to negative performance reviews and being passed over for key projects. Professionally, interrupting my engineers in one-on-ones strains those relationships, while personally, the extreme jitteriness during my kids' school assemblies or waiting in lines makes it hard to just relax. It is definitely much harder to manage now in these highly structured environments compared to when I was just doing hands-on coding.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me at what age you first started noticing these symptoms of restlessness, impulsivity, and difficulty waiting for your turn, and have they been present consistently throughout your life?\n\nPatient: Yes, they have actually been present since I was a child. Back in elementary school, teachers were always telling my parents that I couldn't stay in my seat, blurted out answers, and constantly walked around the classroom when I was supposed to be working quietly. It's definitely been a consistent, lifelong pattern for me.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been diagnosed with or treated for any other conditions, such as mood disorders, anxiety disorders, or learning disorders, that could be contributing to your symptoms of inattention and impulsivity?\n\nPatient: No, I have never been diagnosed with or treated for any other conditions like anxiety, mood disorders, or learning disabilities. This is actually the first time I've ever sought out any kind of psychiatric evaluation or mental health treatment.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned that these symptoms have been present since childhood, but can you tell me if there was ever a period in your life where your symptoms significantly improved or decreased, even if temporarily?\n\nPatient: I don't think there was ever a time they truly went away or improved. However, they were definitely less of a problem and easier to manage when I was working in fast-paced startup environments doing hands-on coding.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that your symptoms have been present since childhood, but can you clarify if you've experienced any periods of significant improvement or worsening of these symptoms during adolescence or early adulthood, before your current senior role?\n\nPatient: I don't recall any specific periods of significant improvement or worsening during my adolescence or early adulthood. I think I mostly just got by because my environments, like school and my earlier startup jobs, naturally allowed me to stay active and multitask.\n\nDoctor: Can you compare the severity of your symptoms, such as restlessness and impulsivity, in childhood versus adulthood, and how have they impacted your functioning in different life settings?\n\nPatient: In childhood, the symptoms were highly visible, with teachers constantly complaining that I couldn't stay in my seat, walked around, and blurted out answers. As an adult, I coped well for years in fast-paced coding roles, but since my promotion two years ago, the restlessness and impulsivity have resurfaced as major issues. Now, leaving my seat in long meetings and interrupting in one-on-ones has seriously impacted my professional functioning, leading to negative performance reviews and missed career opportunities.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe any instances where you engaged in physical activities that could be considered excessive or inappropriate for the setting, such as running or climbing in inappropriate situations?\n\nPatient: I don't literally run or climb on things anymore as an adult, but I experience the adult equivalent, which is an intense, pent-up physical restlessness. During long meetings or my kids' school assemblies, I get this jittery feeling like I'm going to crawl out of my skin, forcing me to constantly get up, stretch, or pace around.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your symptoms have impacted your social relationships, such as friendships and romantic relationships, and have you noticed any differences in how your symptoms affect these relationships compared to your professional relationships?\n\nPatient: Honestly, I haven't really noticed a major impact on my personal friendships or romantic relationships. My friends and family are quite used to my high energy, so the difficulties I've been experiencing are almost entirely focused on my professional life and work environment.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your difficulties with restlessness and impulsivity are more prominent than your difficulties with inattention and disorganization, or are they equally problematic for you?\n\nPatient: The restlessness and impulsivity—specifically my constant urge to leave my seat during meetings and my habit of jumping in with answers—are definitely much more prominent and cause the most disruption at work. While I do also struggle with my attention drifting and organizing my weekly tasks, those issues feel secondary to the physical need to move.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate the proportion of your daily life where you feel your restlessness and impulsivity symptoms are under control versus when they are problematic, and how does this impact your overall functioning?\n\nPatient: When I am doing hands-on coding, I feel completely in control, but since transitioning to my senior role two years ago, a large portion of my day is filled with long meetings where my restlessness is highly problematic. This has really impacted my functioning at work, leading to performance reviews noting that I seem distracted and disengaged. I've even been passed over for leading high-visibility projects because of how I come across in those sessions.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your symptoms of restlessness and impulsivity have caused more significant problems in your life compared to symptoms of inattention, or are they equally troublesome for you?\n\nPatient: The restlessness and impulsivity are definitely more troublesome because they are highly visible and have directly harmed my professional reputation, leading to me being passed over for leadership roles when I leave my seat or blurt out answers. In contrast, my inattention symptoms, like drifting off during Zoom calls, are frustrating but feel much more internal and are easier to hide from my colleagues.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify whether your symptoms of restlessness and impulsivity have caused significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning, and if so, to what extent?\n\nPatient: Yes, they have caused significant occupational impairment over the last two years. My performance reviews have started to note that I seem distracted and not fully present in meetings because of my restlessness. I've even been passed over to lead high-visibility projects because my managers worry about how I come across during long planning sessions.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your restlessness and impulsivity symptoms would be considered mild, moderate, or severe in terms of how much they interfere with your daily life and work, and can you give me some specific examples to support your answer?\n\nPatient: I would consider my symptoms to be mild overall, but they have recently caused noticeable setbacks at work. Specifically, my performance reviews have noted that I seem distracted or not fully present in meetings, and I've been passed over for leading high-visibility projects because my managers worry about my presence during long planning sessions.\n\nDoctor: Can you elaborate on what you mean by considering your symptoms 'mild overall' despite acknowledging they have caused significant occupational impairment and impacted your professional reputation?\n\nPatient: I consider them mild because I am still highly capable and very successful at my core technical work, like hands-on coding. They only feel significant now because my new senior role demands long, structured meetings and leadership presence, which clash with these lifelong traits and have caused these recent setbacks.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if there are any specific situations or environments where your symptoms of restlessness and impulsivity are less problematic, and if so, what factors in those situations help mitigate their impact?\n\nPatient: My symptoms were much less of a problem when I was doing hands-on software development, particularly in fast-paced startup environments. The coding and rapid problem-solving kept me highly engaged, and my tendencies to pace, move around, and multitask were tolerated and didn't interfere with my performance. It's only in these long, structured planning meetings in my new role that it has become a real issue.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about how often you experience feelings of physical restlessness versus impulsive behaviors, and are there any specific situations where one is more prominent than the other?\n\nPatient: My physical restlessness is most prominent when I am forced to sit still for long periods, like during all-hands meetings or school assemblies, where I get a pent-up, jittery feeling.
